traits.leaf_area_per_basal_area.note: USDA Urban Tree Database (McPherson, van Doorn and Peper 2016, RDS-2016-0005), TS3 raw tree data: its 953 oaks: 0.177 m² of leaf a cm². Median leaf area over trunk area at breast height of its open-grown street and park trees 20 cm or more through, the trees the broadleaf median (0.167) was taken over.

traits.height_growth_rate.note: USDA Urban Tree Database (McPherson, van Doorn and Peper 2016, RDS-2016-0005), TS3 raw tree data, open-grown street and park trees: the median height of its 1,172 oaks of all species (7 age bins, 10 to 100 years) by age bin, fitted (least squares, weighted by trees) as H (1 - exp(-k (age + 3))): k 0.028 a year, H 24.0 m. Bins and fit: plantgen-claude project-files/tree-shape/UTD-SIZES-2026-10-23.md, round5-2026-10-26/tools/utdfit.py (tree shape, 2026-10-27).

traits.crown_spread.note: USDA Urban Tree Database (McPherson, van Doorn and Peper 2016, RDS-2016-0005), TS3 raw tree data: its 677 oaks 25 years or older (13 species): 0.92. Median crown width over height of its trees 25 years or older (15 or older where it has fewer than 10 that old), measured open-grown street and park trees.

traits.crown_base_share.note: USDA Urban Tree Database (McPherson, van Doorn and Peper 2016, RDS-2016-0005), TS3 raw tree data: its 677 oaks 25 years or older (13 species): 0.20 (quartiles 0.15 and 0.26). Median height of the crown's base over the tree's height of its trees 25 years or older (15 or older where it has fewer than 10 that old), measured open-grown street and park trees, which are often pruned up for clearance.

appearance.bark_look.thickness.note: The genus's bark thickness as its reference species', quercus-garryana (plantgen-claude project-files/bark/records/quercus-garryana.json): text: FOFEM 0.029

appearance.bark_look.stages.young.note: The genus's young stage as its reference species, quercus-garryana, shows it (plantgen-claude project-files/bark/records/quercus-garryana.json): stage: inferred (photo): young trunks of the tree form not described

appearance.bark_look.stages.mature.note: The genus's mature stage as its reference species, quercus-garryana, shows it (plantgen-claude project-files/bark/records/quercus-garryana.json): fissures: text: 'wide ridges and shallow, narrow furrows' (Sudworth); scales: text: 'scaly' (FNA, FEIS); size inferred

traits.terminal_bud.note: Sargent's Manual (sargent-1922, analytical key to the genera, pp. xxiii-xxiv): 'Branchlets with a terminal bud, leaves penniveined. Quercus'; oak buds cluster at the branchlet's tip.

traits.wood_modulus_green_mpa.note: Wood Handbook 2021 (FPL-GTR-282), table 5-3a, green: the range of the 17 Quercus species it tests (black, cherrybark, laurel, northern red, pin, scarlet, southern red, water, willow, bur, chestnut, live, overcup, post, swamp chestnut, swamp white, white), median typical. A species with its own row states its own.

traits.wood_rupture_green_mpa.note: Wood Handbook 2021 (FPL-GTR-282), table 5-3a, green modulus of rupture: the range of the 17 Quercus species it tests (black, cherrybark, laurel, northern red, pin, scarlet, southern red, water, willow, bur, chestnut, live, overcup, post, swamp chestnut, swamp white, white), median typical. A species with its own row states its own.

traits.wood_moisture_green_share.note: Wood Handbook 2021 (FPL-GTR-282), table 4-1: average moisture of green heartwood and sapwood of the Quercus species it lists (California black, northern red, southern red, water, white, willow), as shares of oven-dry mass; the range, median typical.

traits.flowering_position.note: The Woody Plant Seed Manual's oak chapter (read in full): staminate catkins come mostly from the axils of the previous year's leaves and pistillate flowers from the axils of the current year's; FEIS's Quercus garryana review (page read) says the same of the Oregon white oak. No shoot of an oak ends in its flowers.

traits.epicormic.note: Meier, Saunders and Michler (2012, read in full) name oaks the best-studied example of temperate trees whose epicormic buds sit in clusters on the bark and sprout into new shoots; FEIS's Quercus garryana review (page read) reports epicormic sprouts on Oregon white oaks after disturbance and when competing conifers are removed.

traits.self_pruning.note: Devine and Harrington's guide to planting native oaks in the Pacific Northwest (read in full) says an overtopped oak loses vigour and its limbs begin to die; inferred from that, as no source read here uses the words self-pruning.
